overview: Aksum linked the northern Ethiopian highlands to the Red Sea through Adulis. Its monuments and inscriptions reveal a kingdom connected to African and Mediterranean exchange networks. The city also retained religious and ceremonial importance after its political power diminished.

items.text: Stoneworkers carved enormous stelae from single blocks. Some imitate multi-storey buildings, preserving an architectural vocabulary in stone.
The carved stelae belong especially to the third and fourth centuries CE. Royal tombs and later palace ruins reveal several phases of monumental construction.
King Ezana's fourth-century inscriptions used Greek, Sabaean and Ge'ez. Their multiple languages make connections across the region visible.
Christianity was introduced during the fourth century. Church building subsequently became part of the city's sacred landscape.
Adulis connected maritime commerce with inland routes, while ivory trade linked Aksum with Sudan.
Later Ethiopian emperors continued to be crowned at Aksum. Political decline did not erase its ceremonial role.
